d.title: The shape you need decides the verb
d.caption: Four verbs, and the choice is not about what you compute but about what **shape** comes back. Reaching for `apply` when `transform` was meant is the commonest cause of a result that will not assign back to the frame.

d.title: Every unshifted window is a leak
d.caption: A rolling mean at row *t* includes row *t* itself, so a feature built from it has seen its own target. The fix is one call, and forgetting it is the single most common leak in time-series feature code.

items.label: rolling(3).mean() at row t
items.desc: averages rows t-2, t-1 and t — including the present

items.label: so the feature knows its own row
items.desc: and the model scores beautifully in backtest and fails live

items.label: shift(1) first, then roll
items.desc: now the window ends at t-1 and the feature is causal

items.label: check with a one-row sanity test
items.desc: the feature at row t must be computable before row t arrives

d.title: Timezones: the three states a timestamp can be in
d.caption: Naive, UTC-aware and local-aware are different types, and comparing across them raises or silently misleads. Store UTC, convert for display — and remember that a local time can be ambiguous twice a year.
cells: an instant plus a display rule

cells.text: DST makes one hour ambiguous and one absent

d.title: Normalisation: making equal things equal
d.caption: Order matters. Case-folding before stripping leaves trailing spaces in the keys; stripping accents after mapping aliases makes the mapping miss. This sequence is the one that does not need a second pass.

items.label: strip, then collapse inner whitespace
items.desc: “ New  York ” and “New York” are now the same string

items.label: case-fold
items.desc: casefold(), not lower() — it handles more than ASCII

items.label: normalise unicode and strip accents
items.desc: NFKD, then drop the combining marks

items.label: map known aliases last
items.desc: the mapping keys are now in the same normal form as the data

items.label: count distinct before and after
items.desc: it must fall; if it did not, the normalisation did nothing

d.title: query and eval: what they buy and what they cost
d.caption: Both parse a string, which is why they read well and why a typo becomes a runtime error rather than a syntax one. The speed argument only applies past roughly a hundred thousand rows, and only to `eval`.

cells.text: a typo fails at run time

d.title: What the parser decides without asking
d.caption: Every one of these defaults will eventually be wrong for your file. Passing `dtype=` and `keep_default_na=False` turns a class of silent corruption into an explicit decision — the string “NA” as a country code is the classic case.

cells.text: “NA” as a real value becomes NaN

cells: a saved index reappears as Unnamed: 0

d.title: The byte-order mark, and the bug it causes
d.caption: A UTF-8 BOM is three bytes at the start of a file that mean nothing to the content. Read with plain `utf-8` they become part of the **first column name**, so a lookup on that name fails with a message that looks nothing like the cause.

d.title: Rows against columns, and when each wins
d.caption: The layout decides which queries are cheap. Analysis reads a few columns of many rows, which is exactly what columnar storage is for — and exactly what a row format makes expensive.

columns.title: row-oriented — CSV, most OLTP
items: reading three columns still touches every byte
compresses poorly: neighbouring values have different types
right for writing and reading whole records

columns.title: columnar — Parquet, Arrow
items: reading three columns touches only those three
compresses well: a column is one type, often repetitive
carries a schema and per-chunk statistics for pushdown

d.title: The order the engine actually runs
d.caption: Not the order you write it in, and that explains two things at once: why an alias defined in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE, and why WHERE filters rows while HAVING filters groups.

items.label: FROM and JOIN
items.desc: build the working set first

items.label: WHERE
items.desc: filter ROWS — before any grouping exists

items.label: GROUP BY
items.desc: collapse into groups

items.label: HAVING
items.desc: filter GROUPS — which is why it can use an aggregate

items.label: SELECT
items.desc: compute the output columns and their aliases, only now

items.label: ORDER BY, then LIMIT
items.desc: ORDER BY can use a SELECT alias; WHERE never could

d.title: Three ranking functions that are not interchangeable
d.caption: They differ only on ties, and that difference decides whether “the latest row per key” returns one row or several. `ROW_NUMBER` is the one that guarantees exactly one.

d.title: Push the work down, or pull the rows up
d.caption: The database is usually better at filtering and aggregating than your process is, and the wire is the bottleneck. The rule: send as little as possible over it, and read the plan to confirm the predicate actually reached the index.
cells: check the plan uses an index
only if the join is not expressible

cells.text: right, and let it use the index

d.title: The sequence for meeting a dataset
d.caption: In this order, because each step changes what the next one means. Looking at distributions before checking the row count means interpreting a histogram of a truncated export — which has happened to everyone once.

items.label: shape, dtypes and memory
items.desc: is this the whole export, and did anything come in as object?

items.label: missingness, per column and jointly
items.desc: and whether two columns are missing together, which is a clue

items.label: cardinality
items.desc: a key that is not unique, or a category with one value, both matter

items.label: distributions and ranges
items.desc: now the histogram means something; look for impossible values

items.label: relationships and duplicates
items.desc: correlations, and whether the grain is what you were told

d.title: Three correlations, three questions
d.caption: Pearson measures a straight line, Spearman any monotone relationship, Kendall the consistency of orderings. A nonlinear but monotone pair can give Pearson near zero and Spearman near one — which is the case that matters.

d.title: Three mechanisms, and only one is testable
d.caption: The mechanism decides whether dropping rows is safe, and MNAR cannot be distinguished from MAR by the data alone — it needs knowledge of how the data was produced. That is why “why is it missing” is a question for a person, not a test.

d.title: What each fill removes from the data
d.caption: Every simple fill understates variance, because it puts mass at a single point. The indicator column is the cheap defence: it keeps the fact of the gap available to the model even after the gap is filled.

cells.text: variance down, shape pulled to centre

d.title: The four treatments for an outlier
d.caption: Deleting is the default and the worst, because an outlier is often the most informative row you have. The question to answer first is whether it is an error or a fact — and only an error earns removal.
cells: keeps the row, bounds the value
a long tail you do not want to fit

d.title: Two questions decide the encoding
d.caption: Cardinality and whether the model is tree-based. Those two answers pick the encoder, and the third branch is where most of the leakage in a feature pipeline comes from.

root.label: a categorical column
root.sub: how many levels, and which model?

children.label: ordinal codes
children.sub: trees only — implies an order otherwise

children.label: target encoding
children.sub: high cardinality — out-of-fold, or it LEAKS

d.title: The scalers, and what each does to an outlier
d.caption: A single extreme value compresses everything else into a sliver under min-max, which is why it is the wrong default. Robust scaling uses the median and IQR, so the outlier moves far without dragging the rest with it.

d.title: Cyclical encoding, and why a raw hour misleads
d.caption: Hour 23 and hour 0 are one unit apart in time and twenty-three apart as integers, so any model using distance sees midnight as the furthest point from 11pm. Two columns fix it.

items.label: the problem: 23 and 0 are adjacent
items.desc: but a model reads them as maximally far apart

items.label: map the hour onto a circle
items.desc: theta = 2*pi*hour/24

items.label: emit sin(theta) and cos(theta)
items.desc: two columns, and now the distance between 23 and 0 is small

items.label: the same shape for day, month, weekday
items.desc: use the right period: 7, 12, 365 — not always 24

d.title: Three families of feature selection
d.caption: They differ in whether a model is involved and how often. Filters are cheap and ignore interactions; wrappers see interactions and cost a model fit per candidate set — and both leak if the selection happens outside the fold.

d.title: The contract a pipeline enforces
d.caption: The value is not tidiness — it is that `fit` can only ever see training data. Every statistic a transformer learns is learned inside the fold, which is the mechanical prevention of the leak that hand-written preprocessing invites.

items.label: fit learns from the training fold only
items.desc: the mean, the categories, the vocabulary — all from inside

items.label: transform applies what was learned
items.desc: to any data, including the fold it never saw

items.label: cross-validation refits per fold
items.desc: so the statistics are recomputed, which is the point

items.label: and a stateless-looking step is the trap
items.desc: anything that touches the target, or the whole column, is stateful

d.title: Metrics that survive a shifting base rate
d.caption: Accuracy is uninformative under imbalance — at 1% positives, predicting the majority scores 99%. PR-AUC moves with the base rate and ROC-AUC does not, which makes them answer different questions rather than one being better.
